topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: A tree owns its children, while each child needs to find its parent. Making every edge a shared owner seems convenient, but it creates a cycle: the parent keeps the child alive and the child keeps the parent alive. Neither object’s last owner ever disappears.

blocks.text: Smart pointers make particular ownership policies executable. They do not choose the correct policy for the application. HarborWorks might need one owner for a report generator, shared lifetime for an immutable published snapshot, and a non-owning link back to a parent object. Those are three different relationships and should not be collapsed into one pointer type selected by habit.

blocks.text: Begin every design with a graph of ownership. Label an owning edge differently from a borrowing edge. Then trace what happens when one owner disappears. The important question is not whether a pointer looks modern; it is whether the last intended owner can release the resource without leaving a live user behind or retaining a cycle forever.

topics.title: 6.1 Expressing Exclusive Ownership with std::unique_ptr
topics.summary: std::unique_ptr<T> represents exclusive ownership of a dynamically managed object through its deleter. It cannot be copied, because copying would create another exclusive owner. It can normally be moved when responsibility should pass to another owner.

topics.title: 6.1.2 Transferring Unique Ownership
topics.summary: Moving a unique pointer transfers its ownership and leaves the source empty under the library’s specified move behavior. The receiving object now controls destruction. Passing a unique pointer by value to a function therefore makes ownership transfer visible at the call boundary.

blocks.text: A function that only reads the object should usually accept the object by const reference or a documented pointer, not demand ownership transfer. A function that optionally observes it can accept a nullable borrowed pointer. Choose the interface based on the relationship needed by the callee, not merely the representation used by the caller.

blocks.text: A consuming function can take a unique pointer by value. The caller must transfer the pointer explicitly when passing an existing owner. If the function returns normally without storing or returning the owner, the local parameter destroys its pointee. This is often appropriate for a sink operation whose contract includes consumption, but it would be surprising for a function named inspect.

blocks.text: A reference to a unique pointer is a different interface. It can allow the function to replace the caller’s owner through reset or assignment. That authority should be required by the operation, not granted merely because the caller stores its object in a unique pointer. Borrowing the pointee narrows what the callee can do to the lifetime manager.

blocks.text: After a successful move of a unique pointer, the source owner is empty. The pointee itself may remain at the same address under the new owner. A borrower can remain usable only while the transferred object remains alive and its own validity conditions hold. Moving the owner does not grant a borrower permission to outlive the new owner, nor does it transfer the borrower automatically into a different scope.

blocks.text: The ownership group matters more than the numerical address. Creating two unrelated shared pointers from the same raw pointer can create two independent groups that each believe they must destroy the same object. Copy an existing shared pointer when sharing an ownership group; do not reconstruct a new owner from its get() result. The code may appear to work until the groups are destroyed, which makes a direct ownership audit more valuable than waiting for a crash.

blocks.text: The aliasing constructor illustrates the distinction between a stored pointer and an owned lifetime. A shared pointer can expose a subobject while keeping a larger owning object alive through the same control block. This is useful but requires careful understanding: the stored pointer is what dereferencing accesses, while the ownership group determines what stays alive. Do not infer ownership solely from the exposed address.

topics.title: 6.2.2 Recognizing Shared-Ownership Costs
topics.summary: Reference counting adds bookkeeping, and shared lifetime can make destruction happen at an unexpected point when the last owner disappears. The pointee is not automatically thread-safe merely because shared ownership bookkeeping supports certain concurrent operations on separate shared-pointer objects.

cards.question: Explain Recognizing Shared-Ownership Costs in your own words.
cards.answer: Reference counting adds bookkeeping, and shared lifetime can make destruction happen at an unexpected point when the last owner disappears. The pointee is not automatically thread-safe merely because shared ownership bookkeeping supports certain concurrent operations on separate shared-pointer objects.

blocks.text: Avoid using use_count() as a synchronization or exclusive-access proof. Another owner can appear, and the count does not describe raw borrowers. Performance and concurrency requirements need their own design. A shared pointer is a lifetime mechanism, not a mutex, a transaction, or a guarantee that access patterns are race-free.

blocks.text: Shared ownership adds work beyond an ordinary borrow or exclusive transfer. Copying an owner adjusts lifetime bookkeeping; separate object access may involve indirection; destruction of the final owner triggers cleanup at the point where that final ownership disappears. Those costs can be worthwhile when independent consumers genuinely need to keep an object alive.

Those costs can be worthwhile when independent consumers genuinely need to keep an object alive.

blocks.text: The harder cost is conceptual. A resource can remain alive long after the creating function returns because an unrelated callback retained an owner. If that callback is never released, the object remains retained even without a cycle. A memory investigation should therefore identify retained owners as well as allocations. “No raw new” is not evidence that lifetime is bounded as intended.

blocks.text: Shared-pointer lifetime management does not make the pointee’s data thread-safe. Different shared-pointer objects participating in the same ownership group have specified bookkeeping behavior, but unsynchronized writes to a shared mutable report remain a separate concurrency problem. Even a read-only-looking interface can expose mutable nested objects. The single-threaded labs test ownership, not a concurrency guarantee.

blocks.text: Avoid using use_count() as a general permission check for mutation. A numerical observation is not an application synchronization protocol, and the meaning can change as owners are created or destroyed. Prefer explicit exclusive mutation before publication, followed by immutable shared snapshots, when that matches the workload. The supplemental snapshot laboratory demonstrates this separation without introducing threads.

Different shared-pointer objects participating in the same ownership group have specified bookkeeping behavior, but unsynchronized writes to a shared mutable report remain a separate concurrency problem. Even a read-only-looking interface can expose mutable nested objects. The single-threaded labs test ownership, not a concurrency guarantee.

Avoid using use_count() as a general permission check for mutation. A numerical observation is not an application synchronization protocol, and the meaning can change as owners are created or destroyed. Prefer explicit exclusive mutation before publication, followed by immutable shared snapshots, when that matches the workload. The supplemental snapshot laboratory demonstrates this separation without introducing threads.

blocks.text: A weak pointer must be promoted with lock() before accessing an object that may have disappeared. The result is either an empty shared pointer or an owning participant keeping the object alive for the duration of its use. Store the result locally and use that same result. A separate expired() check followed by an unprotected assumption is not the lifetime operation the interface is designed to provide.

blocks.text: Promotion secures the object’s lifetime, not an arbitrary consistency property of its fields. The parent may remain alive while its application state changes. A multithreaded design still needs synchronization for mutable data. In the single-threaded hierarchy example, the important distinction is simply between an available parent and a parent that has been released.

blocks.text: Weak observers can also support caches that should not keep values alive indefinitely. A cache lookup can attempt promotion and recompute a missing value. That policy differs from a cache of strong owners, which retains every stored value until explicit eviction. Write down which retention behavior the application wants before choosing a map’s value type.

A sanitizer may later report double deletion, yet the repair belongs at construction: copy the existing shared pointer or redesign the transfer. Do not run the double-owner defect in the normal suite; reason about the invalid ownership and keep the shipped examples defined.

For immutable report publication, construct the complete snapshot before sharing it, then expose it through a const pointee interface without retaining a mutable alias that bypasses that policy. Const shared ownership is only as strong as the full alias graph permits.

topics.title: Review and solution reasoning
topics.summary: Exclusive ownership can coexist with borrowing. Shared ownership duplicates lifetime participation, not the pointee’s value. Weak observation breaks an owning cycle only when it replaces the appropriate strong edge. A smart pointer can enforce a selected policy, but the application must still define mutation rights, retention boundaries, and what failure means.
